item.dc:creator: Sean Forde
item.content:encoded:
So, for those of you who don’t know,

I have terrible stage freight.

That may sound surprising considering I spent more than 20 years playing music and more than 15 years teaching in various ways.

Look at me now, though, my hair’s all out of sorts . . .

Another thing you may not know is that I’ve been on a mental health leave for some time now. It’s been really good for me. It’s helped me connect with my family and my children. And Thank God for that!

Been playing music again around the house. And I’m enjoying it. We’ve been homeschooling the kids and so I’ve also dubbed it our music class, which feels a little bit like I’m slam-dunking a bunch of newbies. What can I say? It’s been a while.

I love them so much. My kids. I consider them my gurus. They see things we can’t. We’re getting better at listening to them (I think? I hope?)


. . . and then Noah said . . .

“Dad, you should record that and post it”, I said

“. . .”

well, I hesitated, but then I said,

“Ok, but I want to leave everything else as is.” Meaning, if someone claps, if one of the dogs bark, if someone gets a phone notification or whatever, I want to capture that stuff too.

This was our first living room recording and it was captured via Voice Memo. This was the song Noah suggested.

It’s not perfect, but I love it. It shows how much I enjoy music when in my own safe spaces. And it shows there’s something to be said for vulnerability. At least I like to think so. And I’m trying to model it for my kids.

item.dc:creator: Sean Forde
item.content:encoded:
I have tried to use AI in all sorts of ways, and with good intentions, but being a teacher myself, I’ve always been super cautious of plaguerism.

Having taught songwriting
posted “play-along videos”
and sing-along mp3s before that
and being a songwriter myself

I think AI remains a choice . . .

As a songwriter, I love wrestling with words, just as I love wrestling with melody. Even more, I love the way words and melody wrestle with one another. That’s prosody.

I would never CHOOSE to give that work away. But after 100s of takes in a home studio, and 100s of hours spent mixing and editing . . .
When it’s mastering time, I’m changing my tune.

When that happens, please gimme a shot of AI . . . PLEASE!

That’s not so for all music makers. Some love to mix and some love to master. Why deprive them of the work they wish to offer this world?

A New Kind of Time Capsule

It may seem strange, but I’ve never been big on pictures. I don’t know. There’s something in me that’s just doesn’t always like em.

The way I see it, we hear the world before we have eyes. And so I’m seeing these recordings as my own “pictures”. Like little time capsules, but in a truer sense than the old box in the ground.

My New North

Here on out, I plan on starting over and releasing all my creative stuff here. What you’ll find:

  1. Home-Recorded Songs

    1. Songs I’ve never released

    2. Songs I have previously released and have taken down from all platforms

    3. New songs. I’ve got some home studio gear still and I’d like to play with it again.

  2. Demos:

    1. New songs, already fixed in some tangible medium of expression, but being played live being captured by the phone (demos)

  3. Improvs:

    1. An audio clip being improvised as it’s being recorded

  4. Other art stuff

  5. Covers:

    1. I’d like to share some songs I love, and maybe talk about them too.

    2. Some may be requests from my kids. Both of whom wish to be gamers and content creators. Pray for me . . .

item.title: Old Song: Clean That Face
item.dc:creator: Sean Forde
item.content:encoded:
My Friend Jon

After high school, I went to NYU and my horizons blossomed. Most of it in the school bookstore or school library, but I made a few friends my freshman year.

Two of which were my neighbors, Andy and Jon.

Jon and I could talk about movies or music for hours. First time back home, I had 4 pages of like 300 movies I hadn’t seen.

My sister Tara and I went to our local library and tried to watch as many of them as possible.

Remember that movie, pumpkin, Tara? That one sure was different.

Jon also introduced me to lots of music. He was a huge Billy Joel fan, and being a Long Islander, it’s baked into my DNA, so we started off on solid footing. Most importantly, he introduced me to musicals.

A Chorus Line
1776
Pippen

His brother wrote musicals and was also super duper talented.

To me though, Jon was the real treasure. He knew so so much. And those willing to enter his orbit were transformed by his openness and his kindness.

Jon’s Film

I remember when he was making his first film and asked me to help with the music.

So much had happened in those few years at college that I got myself kinda lost.

His film idea, though, was a great one. Picture this, Sicily 1922 …

Ok, not Sicily, but picture this…

Two pretty looking main character types meet up in the intro and have your Disney-fíed version of a romantic kiss and then it pans up to some fireworks that linger long past their welcome -jokingly so.

The following scene kicks off the real movie, which centers on the guy’s best friend. He starts off with a scraggly beard and is awkward, but is ultimately a really good guy.

A diamond underneath years of rough.

The scene I remember best is when he shaves off the beard and decides to take another shot. Not just another shot at love, but also another shot at being himself.

The song I wrote for that scene is called, Clean That Face, and was set to the character shaving in the mirror.

Think Royal Tenenbaums, but with a Jon Brion hopeful-ness.

Since leaving school, we’ve gone our separate ways as many do.

I know Jon’s still following me and I hope he knows I’ve got him in my heart as well.

It’s because of him I love Directors just as much as films.

The film contained mostly incidental music, but this was one of the exceptions.

item.dc:creator: Sean Forde
item.content:encoded:
Even broken clocks are right twice a day.

It doesn’t mean they work, but it also means nothing is ever fully broken.

When the world’s on fire, some artists point at the fire.
Cause some people are still asleep
and sometimes, you know, we need a smoke alarm.

Sometimes, though, we need to chill. Like really mellow yellow level chill.

John Lennon loved Donovan and so do I, but man, that mellow yellow song’s problematic as Bleeeeeeep!

but he also wrote catch the wind. Sorta an answer to Dylan’s blowin’ in the wind.

Like some lilywhite yin and yang or somethin

Donovan also taught me about Buffy St. Marie. And the song Universal Soldier.

I don’t know what I’m trying to say, really. Maybe I’m just tired of burning all my heroes.

I don’t know what any of these guys have done and I hope it wasn’t too bad. I’m sure some of it is. And for that, they do need to go. But I’d also like to hang on to some of the good they put in the world too.

All I want to do right now is have some fun. Ha, Sheryl Crow’s really pretty amazing, isn’t she? And so was Eric Clapton, but that Tears in Heaven song ripped me to pieces growing up.

It was the first finger-picking song I ever learned on guitar. The sheet music was given to me by you know who. Isn’t it ironic? Doncha think? . . . a little too ironic. And I really do think!

Still, it taught me an empathy so so deep I just can’t shake no matter how hard I try. Trust me, swifties, I’ve tried to shake it off so so many times.

Pheobe Bridgers feels it too. And we’re not alone. Try some Bright Eyes, or some Bon Iver, or even some Pavement.

the list goes on and on and on and on . . .

For right now, for me and my pa, and for all the pas going too early, I just need a little Tom Petty . . .

You belong among the wildflowers
You belong in a boat out at sea
Sail away, kill off the hours
You belong somewhere you feel free

Got an old song I’d like to share here. Don’t know if it’ll ever make any money, but who cares anymore . . . I think I just need to try and get this clock a little less broken.

at least for a little while . . .

If anyone out there wants to learn it, please play it for me. y’all are better at following threads than i am

Call Me Mr. Fashionably Late

One of the hardest lessons I ever had to learn was . . .

Uncertainty is good and so are people.

It’s one of the toughest lessons because life gets in the way. And when life gets in the way, the stress hits the fan and it gets everywhere.

But . . .

When you’re down and out, like really down and out, it’s also the only way to get up and out.

I’ve met so many talented songwriters and musicians in my life. All super talented. None are famous cause this world aint too good and letting the good ones get found. Sad, but they’re out there. You just have to go out and find em.

And when you find one, it’s on you to spread the word. Word or mouth is the way art spreads, not media. Well, media can be used to spread the word too, but like I said above . . . life gets in the way. For everyone. Everywhere. All the time. Like that movie

Everything Everywhere All At Once!

I mean, come on. That rock scene is just so so brilliant!

More Yada Yada

Anyway, I know I go on . . .

I’ve known so many guitarists out there and so many of them are just awesome. I could never play fast. It’s like my kryptonite.

For me, I’d rather sing, or make an instrument try to sing.

The greatest guitarist I’ve ever met was named Josh. His is not my story to tell, but man, could he play. If you’re curious, check him out here:

We even played this show in Queens at a bar that was “rescued” by the TV show Bar Rescue. Oh, John you little taffer, you.

item.title: New Song (Demo): Who Is Affected By You?
item.dc:creator: Sean Forde
item.content:encoded:
I used to have lots of songs online.

Spotify, Apple Music, and yada yada. Never had much luck putting my stuff out there, though, no matter how I pitched it. No matter how hard I tried, where I tried, or how much money I could put into the process. My dad was one of the only people I knew who actively shared it around with his friends. I miss him. And I think about him every day.

Even helped me into a band of lawyers aptly named Equity. And they were really great. Once the kids came, it got harder to keep up considering everything going on at the time. And after the pandemic, the keyboard player helped me find another band who was also great.

Without a big social media presence, most places don’t take you seriously. Reminds you how much of the world, from elementary school all the way up the corporate ladder, is just a glorified popularity contest masquerading as merit.

And social media, too, feels alien to me. I love connecting with other people, but the timelines, the endless scrolling, and the algorithms all get in the way of real connection. It’s like the curate the connection possibilities for you. And if you’re not an exhibitionist or some voyeur, the world thinks you must be nuts.

Well, this nut is done with Social Media. At least for now. Same with Spotify, YouTube, and every other platform promising the world and leaving songwriters with nothing but penance. It’s too much for me to balance right now and I need balance like nobody’s business.

For now . . .
Forget the playlists
Forget the stupid streams
And forget the polish. ALL OF IT!

Here’s a demo of a song with my instructions on how to play it. It’s how I like to write and record. Just go for it and iterate till ya feel good.

i refuse to polish turds

Michelle, you don’t have to explain yourself to me
Others just don’t know what to do with you
You’re out of control in all the best ways
Goodness let loose from a cage of self-hatred

I know the feeling
Been there myself
Not in the same ways
We are all unique

Life is universal
With furniture sprinkled in
We choose the stuff
The esque-ish-ness of life

Love is like an elephant
And remember love is blind
The only way is to feel
One small piece at a time

So close your eyes and reach your hands
With faith around your heart

I promise I will do the same
But know that I will fall
Cause love is also a balance beam
Tugging side to side

Not me
Not you
Who Me?
Who You?
No me
No you

And everybody falls

But the hardest lessons of love
I’ve ever had to learn
Is to see the love come back around
And feeling all the burn
Waiting for you . . . in return

Cause love will kill
And love will hurt
But so do we all
Again and again

Hurt people hurt people
“Everybody knows”
But loved people love people
From their hair down to their toes

haikukus

Ladies, please protect
The sweetness emerging in
Our lonely male worlds

Fellas, trust yourselves
A bite to find the sweetness
In the darkest parts of you

item.title: Um . . . No, Thank You
item.dc:creator: Sean Forde
item.content:encoded:
There are so many little-known facts about life. Not factual in the clinical sense. But apparent in more of a relational sense.

Uninterrupted time with your spouse is hard to come by.
Uninterrupted time with your children is hard to come by.
Responsibilities take over.
Life gets busy.

And, the worst of all . . . gratitude and positivity are key when interacting with others.

I’ve been told many variations of this.

Be grateful.
Be positive.
Look at everything you have.
Look at everything we’ve given you.

My mind thinks back to the Beatles’ “She’s Leaving Home”.

We gave her most of our lives
Sacrificed most of our lives
We gave her everything money could buy
She’s leaving home, after living alone, for so many years

Recently, my mom brought our whole family to Ireland. It was for “Dad” she claimed.

Ireland certainly is beautiful. Almost offensively so. You could have a nervous breakdown beside the Cliffs of Moher and still find yourself wondering, “Well, isn’t this lovely.”

My mother put an enormous amount of work into that trip. Money too. She planned hotels, flights, meals. She planned everyone’s photographs and memories for them too.

All right, is everyone good and listening?
I AM GRATEFUL!
There. I said it . . .

Can I speak now?

Because that’s the part nobody wants to talk about. Sometimes gratitude is gratitude. And it’s beautiful. Sometimes, though, it’s a cover charge.

You may enter this family, this workplace, this classroom, this country, provided that you first acknowledge how lucky you are to be here.

Um . . . no, thank you.

I Get a Vote

We’ve gotten so good at talking about consent in one part of human life.

And Holy shit.
Took us long enough.

If someone does something to your body that you don’t want, your desire matters. Your “no” matters. Your silence doesn’t magically become a yes simply because the other person had “good intentions.”

But there’s an even larger question underneath consent that doesn’t go away when we’ve got our clothes on.

Do I get a vote in what happens to me?
Do I get to say this doesn’t feel good?
Am I really allowed to say I don’t want this?

And when do I get to say that the thing you insist you’re doing for me is actually something that you want?

Gifts are a great example of this divide.

Do I get to experience a gift differently from the giver?
Am I allowed to tell my mother that the vacation she remembers as an extraordinary act of love didn’t feel that way to me?

Or does the price tag settle the argument?
Apparently some receipts are long enough to become gag orders.

The Gratitude Economy

My mother loves gifts.
She likes vacations.
She likes Christmas.
She likes helping.
She likes saving people.

And for a long time I accepted that this is simply her “love language.”
Maybe it is.
But I thought love was a language with at least two people in the conversation.

If I spend forty years speaking French to someone who keeps telling me they don’t understand French, eventually I have to consider the possibility that I’m not really communicating.

Maybe it’s just that I really like speaking French.

My mother gave us a lot. Everything that money could buy. But there were so many things I desperately wanted that never cost anything.

Like attention.
Curiosity.
Affection.

And ever more deeply . . .

Permission to be unhappy.
Permission to disagree.
Permission to say, “This isn’t helping me.”

I can’t remember the last time my mom hugged me. And I haven’t really celebrated my birthday for decades. Frankly, I barely remember anything from my childhood.

Hard to tell how much of it was mine.

Money is great at buying things.
It sucks at hugging.

The Men Who Do

I watched my father work. A regular Willie Loman type. All the way to the end.

He left the seminary to become a lawyer. To provide for my mother and his children. He carried student loans for years. He built a career. He did the respectable things. Again and again and again and again.

My father became, in many ways, a human doing instead of a human being.

And I grew up in what remained of the family. Where there was plenty of room for what men could provide . . . and way less room for what a man could actually be. All the while being told otherwise. Like every day was opposite day.

Men could work.
Men could earn.
Men could carry.
Men could fix.
Men could protect.
Men could shut up.

I don’t want it anymore.
Not for myself, and not for my children.

I don’t want them learning that being manly means being useful. Measured, of course, by how little others worry about you.

And I don’t want them learning the inverse lesson either: that care means deciding what another person needs and punishing them when they don’t experience it as love.

Let’s Make Some People Uncomfortable

So yes, I am going to name some people.

Rich people.
Boomers.
Trump voters.
My mother.
People who preach gratitude while showing so little curiosity for others’ experiences.

It’s too easy to call this all hypocrisy. It’s more complicated.

These aren’t interchangeable categories.
Not every Boomer is rich.
Not every wealthy person behaves the same way.
Not everyone who voted for Donald Trump has the same motivation.

Obviously, my mother isn’t personally responsible for the conditions of the US, but everywhere I look, I see people afraid of “generalizing”. So afraid, in fact, that we use individual exceptions to avoid discussing patterns at all. And so we never learn.

You see, naming a pattern is not the same thing as declaring every person inside a category guilty.

It’s about asking where power is located:

Who has money?
Who owns the house?
Who runs the company?
Who controls the classroom?
Who makes the rules?
Who gets the microphone?
Who’s called “negative” when they object?

. . . and who gets reminded to be grateful.

Donald Trump didn’t invent coercion despite the meaning of his family’s assumed name. He didn’t create wealth inequality, family dysfunction, or emotional neglect either. But I refuse to accept that he is irrelevant to the culture of Americans right now.

How? I can accept policy disagreements (mostly), but I cannot forgive his abuse of the bully pulpit.

Presidents possess a platform. And like it or not, their words matter. Their behavior matters. What they reward and what they normalize matters too.

Americans should be allowed to examine all of this without pretending that one man hasn’t somehow crawled inside the country's nervous system.

The same goes for generations.

Older Americans never held a secret meeting deciding how to ruin the future, but come on. Clearly the concentration of wealth, property, and institutional authority are forms of power holding and power wielding.

And whether anyone likes it or not, we are all allowed to talk about that.

In fact, we better.

Positivity Is Not a Moral Virtue

I like positive people. Most my life, I have tried to remain positive. And I carry 40 years of masked tension to prove it.

Thing is, I also like fire alarms. And fire alarms are extremely negative.

Nobody has ever heard one screaming at three in the morning and thought, “God, this thing really needs to work on its gratitude.”

It’s just information. And sometimes information looks like negativity. Sometimes it looks like anger. Sometimes it looks like depression.

Think of the people in your world. Really be curious.

Is every miserable employee lacking resilience?
Is every miserable child in need of an attitude adjustment?

Sometimes the miserable family member isn’t ruining Christmas and birthdays. Sometimes something is wrong.

I tell my children to “Be curious, not critical”. This is so hard to do. So modeling requires a ton of self-work.

That is the part I think we’ve lost.

Curiosity.
Not positivity.
Not gratitude.
Curiosity.

Oprah has an amazing book called “What Happened to You?” I wish everyone would read it if only to jump-start a conversation with themselves, their families, and the impact on those around them.

My favorite songwriter is John Lennon, and his song Imagine has long been met with criticism. Here’s how I would apply my own curiosity to his sentiment.

Imagine asking, “What Happened To You?” before offering advice.

Imagine a parent asking it.
Imagine a boss asking it.
Imagine a teacher asking it.
Imagine a doctor asking it.
Imagine a president asking it.

And now imagine actually waiting for the answer . . . no matter how long it takes.

I’m Done Pretending

I am grateful for many things that my mother has given me.
And I am angry about the many things I didn’t receive.

Both are true.

Ireland was beautiful.
And I was hurting.

Both are true.

My childhood contained wonderfully privileged moments.
And there was desperate emotional hunger in my house.

Both are true.

My father provided for us his whole life.
And I wish that someone had asked what it was costing him.

Both are true.

My mother loves me.
And I don’t experience most of what she calls love as love.

Both are true.

That’s what consent means to me.

Not permission to do whatever the hell I want. I’ve never wanted that anyway. I’ve only ever wanted permission to remain the author of my own experience. And I don’t think I’m unique in that.

You can offer me something.
But only I get to decide whether I want it.

You can help me.
But only I can tell you whether or not it helps.

You can love me.
But you don’t get to dictate the terms and conditions.

Speaking of terms and conditions:
You can give me money.
But you’re not getting my silence, my agency, or my complicity in return.

Because I’m done pretending.
I just can’t take it anymore.

For myself.
For my children.
For my father.
For my family.

And yes, even for my country.
If that sounds negative, I hope you’ll forgive me.
Can’t force stuff like that, y’know.

As for what I do want . . .
I’m trying to be positive enough to believe we can do better.

item.title: Don't Answer It!!
item.description: We treat every interruption like a demand. What if some interruptions aren't asking for our attention, but are offering theirs?
item.dc:creator: Sean Forde
item.content:encoded:
I've been thinking about an idea for weeks now. It kept showing up in unexpected places. First work. Then parenting. Then marriage. Then therapy, music, and teaching.

. . . interruptibility.

Eventually, it showed up in a text message I found myself sending.

“No need to respond. Just wanted you to know I was thinking about you.”

I hit send. And before I’d even received a reply, I noticed something. It felt good.

We Think We Know What Interruptions Are

We’re surrounded by interruptions. First my phone. Then my dogs. Then work requests.

My phone interrupts me to let me know that Gary, the guy I sat next to in some college class, has accepted a new position. Meanwhile, someone I actually love can spend three days wondering whether I disappeared.

The thing is, I don’t think interruptions are the problem. The problem is that we treat them all the same. And it’s our treatment that I’ve been stuck questioning.

We’ve become so accustomed to interruptions asking something from us that we close off. And for me, I’m trying to remember another possibility.

What if an interruption isn’t asking for my attention? What if it’s offering someone else’s?

Not Every Interruption Is Asking for Something

A notification says,

“Look at me.”

A friend checking in says,

“I’m looking at you.”

Both are interruptions, and both can happen at any time, on any day. With so many notifications I’ve got a mosquito net around my attention at all times. Can’t let anything take anything from me . . .

But if not all interruptions are bad, how do I remove the mosquito net and start asking . . .

What is this interruption trying to do?

Staying on Someone’s Radar

Often, people in mosquito nets are treated at a distance. People say,

“Just give them space.”

Good advice. Sometimes. But I don’t think they’re really asking for zero interruptions. And if we’re confusing space with something empty or unaccompanied, we send the impression that their life is theirs to bear alone.

Technology is great at reminders, but it can’t really remind us of our worth. And without that, how do I know which relationships are being kept up by reciprocity and which by the algorithm?

It can be unclear what action to take, but giving someone space doesn’t mean taking them off our radar.

Sometimes love looks like stepping back, sure. Giving room to breathe. Resisting the urge to solve, persuade, or manage. But it doesn’t mean becoming absent. In fact, I think the healthiest relationships keep sending tiny signals.

Not demands. Just reminders.

“I’m here.”

“I saw that.”

“I’ve been thinking about you.”

Because love requires noticing. Not only noticing the other person, but noticing ourselves in relation to one another.

Interruptions That Accompany

Think about a good conversation. And I stress “good”. We interrupt one another constantly. Not by cutting each other off. By nodding and smiling. Saying, “Mm-hmm.” And by leaning forward just a little.

These signals don’t even feel like an interruption. They feel like accompaniment. They reassure us that someone is still there.

Ever talk to someone who never changed expression? Never acknowledged what you were saying? Never even the accompanying “uh-huh.”? Have you ever been that person? I know I have.

Technically, I don’t interrupt. But in conversation, I can disappear.

I’m learning, but I think that learning, too, depends on interruptibility. Every teacher interrupts. Their job depends upon introducing possibilities.

And all lessons seem to begin the same way. With reality refusing to fit the story we’re currently telling ourselves.

Curiosity is an interruption.
So is surprise.
So is a child saying,

“Come look at this.”

The Signal I Meant to Send

I don’t think interruptibility is about becoming available to every interruption. It’s more about pausing and asking what an interruption is trying to do.

And sometimes the most loving interruption asks nothing of us except to remember that we’re still on someone’s radar.

Maybe that's what I discovered when I hit send.

Continue the Thread

  • When has a small interruption (a question, a glance, a text, a pause) changed the direction of your day?

  • What makes you feel genuinely interruptible? What makes you close off?

item.title: Come Look With Me
item.description: A folk song, a wooden ring, and a memory of my father became an unexpected invitation back to myself. An essay about music, inheritance, marriage, and the quiet ways we teach one another how to notice.
item.dc:creator: Sean Forde
item.content:encoded:
There I was, whittling, which has become a pastime for me and the boys.

I was working on a wooden ring for Noah, something he could actually wear. Instead of whittling alongside, Dylan and Noah sat beside me on their iPads, each happily on their own little planet.

The radio was on when Don’t Think Twice, It’s Alright came on.

Not the Dylan version (the one I know inside and out), but Peter, Paul and Mary’s.

It felt fresh for a moment. Not the first time I heard it though. Once the vocal harmonies came in, I was back in my dad’s black Nissan.

Music’s strange like that. Like teleportation.

One second you’re sitting on the couch whittling a ring, and the next your body catches a memory before your mind does.

The Song

We spend a lot of time listening to music in cars.

Long car rides, for me, were opportunities to enjoy albums from beginning to end without interruption.

Neither my mom nor my dad listened that way. Mom liked whatever was current with the occasional classical or musical thrown in. Driving with her, she’d smile, maybe sing along, but the attention was elsewhere. The road, presumably.

Dad was a forever-patron of the Oldies station. Driving with him, he’d tell me about the songs. Not always, but I loved music and often asked. I remember the times he stayed with me and answered.

He loved the Drifters, the Beach Boys, and Jimmy Buffet, but every so often he revealed a soft spot for singalongs and folk music. There was something more to it he seemed to notice. Probably the Irish in him.

I remember him showing me Where Have All the Flowers Gone? He wanted me to notice how the lyrics worked, how they circled back on themselves. There was a logic to it if you paid attention.

Or Seven Drunken Nights. He wanted to make sure I was in on the joke.

He told me he sang Sloop John B. with friends in high school. Nothing more formal than a jukebox at a hangout spot and I don’t think he thought he was especially good. Never the point. He just loved being part of it.

Looking back, I think I get the poetry from him. He understood what songwriters were trying to say.

Or maybe more accurately...

...he understood that they were trying to say something worth noticing. And that it was worth paying attention.

Staying in the Car

When the song ended, I immediately hit replay.

Not to hear it again, but to try again. To get back in my father’s car.

When I find a pathway to a memory I haven’t held in a long time, I don’t want to lose it. I want to sit with it.

As Dylan’s lyrics wandered, so did my mind. Who was my father hearing when this song played?

My mom?
His mom?

Who was I hearing now?

Pretty soon, the song stopped being about goodbyes and became the ways we abandon ourselves.

Many memories of sitting in the car with the music on, I attended to the songs. To what they were trying to do.

It’s like my dad’s way of seeing has rubbed off on me. Now, looking back, I wonder if that was his goal. An invitation into his way of seeing.

Where meaning hides inside of the ordinary.

And when I put out my first album, he asked to put it on so we could listen together. My songs have always been autobiographical and this was one of the rare times I remember feeling seen.

I knew he was really looking.

I Think This Is When People Reach Out

Somewhere during the second play-through, my whittling knife slipped from my hand and tears fell to the ring.

Noah and Dylan kept playing on their tablets, each off on their own planet.

Shay, however, immediately understood the assignment. She climbed the couch, licked my face, and leaned into my chest.

I felt a heaviness in my chest that I wanted to understand (not that understanding has a stellar track record).

I opened the basement door to go downstairs, where I’ve gotten into the habit of thinking through things by myself.

By the third step, I stopped.

“I think this is when people reach out.”

Silence.

I had to put the pieces of this basic act together manually.

It isn’t my default.

And then I thought. That’s really weird. Like dialogue from Resident Alien.

Keeping with the process, I asked myself, “What am I protecting?”

The best I could come up with is, “Michelle’s going to be annoyed.” I stopped again.
”But is that true?”
“I don’t actually have evidence for that. It’s more like it just feels so true.”

And then, like preparing for a band-aid rip, I told myself, “I guess I’ll give it a shot.”

The Way Back

I walked into the bedroom where Michelle was looking at house listings on her phone.

Right away, she started talking about one she’d found. She was excited.

I laid down beside her,

“I had a big moment.”

I’m trying to be direct with what I say and what I feel. I’m not always that clear though and when it comes out, I feel like a child.

I told her about Don’t Think Twice, my father’s car, and the heaviness. And we cried.

She looked at me and said,
“You don’t have to figure any of this out.”

She wasn’t trying to solve anything.
Just accepting an invitation.
I think that’s how relationships deepen.
An ongoing exchange of invitations. To pull into each other’s inner worlds.

And more importantly, it was what I needed to hear. Usually, that’s my brain trying to figure things out.

After a while just holding one another, I said:

“Coming up here, I don’t think I figured any of it out... but I do feel better. It feels lighter.”

“Sure you don’t want to rethink the ‘lighter’ part?”

At some point Shay had climbed into bed with us, having decided personal space was optional.

Come Look With Me

Maybe children don’t only inherit money. Maybe they inherit ways of paying attention.

And maybe they inherit the questions their parents couldn’t answer. Couldn’t even quite put into words.

I heard a song because of my dad and that song made me cry.
That crying became an opportunity to walk toward my wife.
And our marriage became just a little deeper.

His way of paying attention didn’t end with him.
It moved through me into someone else.

In a strange way, my father was still introducing someone he loved to something beautiful.

Only this time...
It wasn’t a lyric.

Later that afternoon, I picked the ring back up and kept carving. I showed Noah where I was at so he could see the detail.

Maybe that’s all inheritance really is.
Someone you love. Teaching you how to notice.

Then one day, without realizing it, you realize you’ve been noticing that way too. And it has served you well.

The Ring

Listen Along

If you’d like to sit in my father’s car for four minutes, here’s the recording:

Continue the Thread

For anyone who’d like to share their magnifying glass to let us into their world:

  • What’s one ordinary thing (a song, smell, recipe, place, or whatever) that still holds someone you love?

  • What’s something you understand now that someone was quietly trying to show you years ago?

item.title: Fatherhood | He Was Just Sitting There
item.description: We often think we know the people closest to us. But what if the labels we've given them have quietly replaced our curiosity? A Father's Day reflection on roles, delight, and the stories we tell about one another.
item.dc:creator: Sean Forde
item.content:encoded:
Every June, fathers everywhere are asked the same question.

“What do you want for Father’s Day?”

This, I think, is our first mistake. It’s not a bad question. It’s because of what happens next.

“What do you want?”

“Oh . . . nothing.”

And if not nothing, the answer is always something comically small.

But the moment a father says, “Nothing,” something fascinating happens. No one hears an answer. They hear a problem. And since problems invite solutions, everyone becomes a detective.

Thinking to themselves:

What’s wrong?

Is he depressed?

Has he always been emotionally unavailable?

Does he need a hobby?

Has he considered pickleball?

Nobody stops to wonder if maybe he means it. Maybe he doesn’t want another thing.

Not forever. Just til Tuesday.

The Man at the Beach

Got me thinking back to when I was eighteen and I worked at a beach. I sat by a booth checking for town stickers. It was a lonely job, but I read a ton of Vonnegut that summer.

Anyway, every evening just before close, this man would park his car facing the water. I assumed the radio was on, but you couldn’t hear anything.

He sat there for thirty or so minutes and left. Every day.

At first, I only cared about closing up. But pretty soon, I started inventing stories. Affair? Drugs? Secret government operation? Witness protection?

By the second week I realized something disappointing.

Nothing was happening.

The man was just sitting there.

Years later, I became him.

Not at the beach, but at grocery stores. Hardware stores. The driveway. Anywhere, really, with a parking lot and low expectations.

The ignition goes off. The groceries just sit there in the passenger seat. They’re in no hurry. No one’s asking the bananas where they’ve been. The milk needs no help calming down. And the bread’s all good with emotional validation.

For ten minutes, no one needs anything.

And recently it hit me. Someone out there is probably telling themselves a story about me.

Human beings would rather invent a bad explanation than tolerate an unanswered question.

Someone can't simply be sitting in a car.

What Changes His Eyes

We get so busy identifying people that we stop noticing them.

Father.
Provider.
Husband.
Self-Sufficient.
Reliable one.
Strong one.

The labels arrive. The curiosity leaves.

Before long, we’re no longer talking to the person. We’re talking to our idea of them.

And that’s the part I keep coming back to.

Not what a father does.
What delights him.

Not what he’s responsible for.
What changes his eyes?

What does he love so much that he loses track of time?

Most people know what a father provides.
Far fewer know what delights him.
Fewer still have asked.

I don’t think that’s a small thing.

Delight isn’t just a feeling. It’s one of the ways we become known. An invitation for others to know us. And an invitation for us to better know ourselves.

When nobody seems interested, the invitation disappears.

You stop bringing it up.
You stop sharing it.
Eventually, you stop assuming it matters.

Then, one day, someone asks what you want for Father’s Day.
You listen carefully.
You really try.
After a while, the role starts answering before you do.

So you say,

“Nothing.”

Which was never really the answer.

It was the clue.

Coda

Next Father’s Day, if he says he wants nothing, don’t rush to explain what he means.

Stay curious a little longer. Maybe he's trying to show you who he is.

Continue the Thread

  1. Who in your life have you become certain you already know?

  2. What story do you think other people have been telling about you?

item.title: Some Meanings Must Be Witnessed
item.description: Hundreds of lost songs. A box of failed floppy disks. A realization that arrived twenty-five years late. Some meanings can be discovered alone. Others require witnesses.
item.dc:creator: Sean Forde
item.content:encoded:
A memory from childhood returned recently.

It came as a feeling in the space around me. Like a feeling, but a transportable one.

It was of me around 13 or so, composing music on the family computer.

I spent so much of my childhood composing music. Lots of it in my head. But when I found Cakewalk around 1994, I was enchanted by how I could write a musical idea, hear it played back to me, and save it for later!

Some of my first breadcrumbs were floppy disks. Entire afternoons converted into tiny digital containers. Thousands of hours of my curiosity and musical growth.

In this memory, though, I remember crouching beneath the desk to reach the floppy drive.

I inserted one into the computer. “Sean’s Songs - 1”.

Waited.

Error.

I tried another.

Error.

Another.

Error.

Something had happened to the disks. The songs were gone. All I remember was feeling heartbroken and helpless.

I cared about those songs. The digital equivalent of my journals in a way.

I told myself, “This must be for the best”.

I can imagine my mom and sisters saying something like that. This came from me though.

And so I did.

. . .

For the next twenty-five years.

The Missing Witness

Looking back, it’s still a puzzle. It never occurred to me to tell anyone.

Not my friends. Not my family.

Those songs occupied thousands of hours of my life. Yet when they disappeared, the only witnesses were the floppy disks themselves.

Which is when I started wondering whether some losses hurt less because the thing is gone...

and more because nobody knew it was there.

For years, I thought I had lost a collection of songs.
Now I think I lost something else.
Records of my becoming. Like traces of me taking shape.
Questions I never knew I was asking and feelings I didn’t know how else to express.

With the exception of a few songs written with friends, nobody saw it happen.
I’m sure my family remembers me hunkered over the computer, but nobody remembers those songs.

Nobody can say, “I really liked that one.”

What Remained

Some meanings can be discovered alone. But not all.

Some meanings must be witnessed.

A joke requires laughter.
A story requires a listener.
Grief requires mourners.
A signal requires somewhere to land.

Without a witness, meanings don’t always fade. The lesson learned was, “don’t expect things to last. All is impermanent.”

Great meaning for a life of endurance. Not much else.

0/10 Stars. Would not recommend.

Carrying

For a long time, I thought I was trying to preserve the songs. Like I didn’t want to forget something I was proud of.

Not because the music was extraordinary.
It wasn’t.
What mattered was the life inside it.

I thought the solution was an archive.
A better backup.
But meaning doesn’t live in floppy disks.
Meaning lives in people.

To witness.
To carry.
To prevent absence from becoming erasure.

Nowadays, with myself and with my family, I’m trying to keep in mind

  1. If something matters to me, share it while it’s alive

  2. If something matters to someone else, witness it while it’s alive

Pick up the Thread

  1. What is something meaningful that almost nobody knows about you?

  2. Tell us about a memory, project, relationship, or experience that mattered more than most people realized. What made it meaningful?

item.title: Participation Precedes Meaning
item.description: As a kid, I disappeared into elaborate internal worlds. This is a reflection on signals, imagination, self-concept, and the uncomfortable realization that participation often precedes meaning.
item.dc:creator: Sean Forde
item.content:encoded:
Looking down on my backyard, you’d see a square of concrete with a basketball hoop, a large stretch of grass with a swing set, and a pool. I was very fortunate.

Not because I loved to swim, dribble, or swing, but because it provided a space for me to get lost in myself.

Where fully orchestrated theme music could follow me up a ladder. Where I could uncover ancient secrets like Indiana Jones. And where I could inhabit the career of some imaginary athlete who would one day receive the recognition he deserved after years of being overlooked.

All internally cinematic.

Looking back, I had an entire internal complex dedicated to the possibility that one day people would finally understand what I had been trying to do all along.

So specific. Most kids were fighting dragons. I was humbly accepting lifetime achievement awards.

Then Somebody Knocked

One day, lost in immersion, I hear a BANG on the backyard gate, followed by a, “Hey Sean! Whatcha doing.”

Simple question, but what do I say? “Oh, you know, just overcoming adversity, silencing critics, and cementing my legacy.”

Visibly, I was huffing and puffing, clutching a pool noodle, near the foot of the slide.

A single knock and it shook me out of my world. And there was shame.

I had been swimming freely in the depths of my imagination only to be summoned, abruptly, to the surface.

This happened a lot. In some ways, I think it made me frightened of the surface. And I don’t want to be anymore.

Meaning is Accumulative

These days I’ve been paying more attention to . . . my attention.

Like the last post, I'm still thinking about signals and I think signals are just things we notice. They can be internal or external and we have choice in which signals we attend to.

And there’s something I keep coming back to about it. The first one doesn’t really mean anything.

Not because of the signal, but because there is nothing yet to compare it to.

Just imagine that first response to a text message. Those three dots appear . . . and disappear. Entire civilizations have collapsed under less certainty.

The first signal is immersive before it can be understood. It just happens to you. Only later does the mind start organizing it around comparisons, patterns, and expectations.

Three conversations later, those three dots come with meaning that’s related to one’s consistency, personality, and conversation style.

In this way, meaning is accumulative

The simplest way it makes sense to me is through rhythm:

One sound is not yet a rhythm.
Two sounds create a space between them.
Three sounds create a pattern you can begin to feel.

In rhythm, additional sounds eventually create tension, release, pulse, expectation, momentum, groove.

At a certain point, it’s not rhythm or even sound. It’s movement and energy.

Meaning works the same way. It doesn’t appear all at once. It accumulates.

Looking back, I think I understood this intuitively. I just wasn’t participating in the same place everyone else was.

Why I Stayed Underwater

Looking at my own signals with this model, I see stuck points. Where I think I’m sending signals, but I’m doing so from a foot under-water.

Kinda obvious to everyone around who’s really in the conversation.

Like that boy immersed in an action sequence running down the slide, the surface sometimes feels out of view.

That is, until I see signals.

. . . attention.

For someone like me who has spent so much time in my own depths, these surface-level interactions don’t feel light. They feel hijacking.

I think I wanted meaning because I wanted certainty.

The world is confusing.
People are confusing.
I am confusing.

So I turned to meaning and became thoughtful.
Then more thoughtful.
Then professionally thoughtful.
Then pathologically thoughtful.

No one wants to spend forty-five minutes interpreting a text message that said:
“Sounds good.” Why’d they put the period, right?

At some point, the strategy began producing the opposite result. The world was confusing, yes, but now even more so.

Beware, the mind’s an escape room.

The real goal for me right now is to be present . . . but also not my default self . . . hmm

Participation Precedes Meaning

Someone like me, stuck in survival attention, needs more than The Power of Now to orient my attention.

This is why I’m trying to remember:

participation precedes meaning.

You have to send the text before knowing how it will be received.
You have to have the conversation before knowing where it will go.
You have to play the rhythm before knowing how it feels.

When I remind myself, “Participation precedes meaning.” It sends a signal that I gotta put something out there otherwise I do not exist. Not in a pursuassive way, but in a logical way.

And for someone trying to develop a self-concept, it’s a reminder . . .
You have to surface before knowing what people will see. Apparently, no focus groups allowed for being yourself.

Unfortunately, I’ve been trying to “figure this out”. Which makes perfect sense. Until it doesn’t.

Because eventually reality rings, sends some new data your way, and reminds you to stop “figuring things out”. It’s like the universe keeps responding:

“Interesting theory. Would you like to interact with another human being now?”

Coming Up for Air

These days I think about Dylan.

Each night, he runs around our kitchen. Imagination firing on all cylinders: some story, some bad guy or mission. Some invisible reality unfolding according to rules known only to him.

I recognize it immediately.

The thing I want most is not to pull him out of that world. I don’t want him to learn that the surface is where imagination goes to be corrected.

I don’t want him to learn that participation means abandoning the depths.

I want him to learn something I’m still learning myself. The goal has never been about choosing between worlds.

It’s about building bridges between them.

Maybe that’s what participation actually is. Like a double paying attention. At yourself and at the other person, both creating a bridge.

Something to cross. To remain reachable.

I spent years looking for meaning like it’s something I could find on my own. It feels like it might be safer that way. Measure twice, cut once. I’m learning life isn’t designed that way.

If you want to know what’s happening, you eventually have to come up for air.

Or maybe, if someone knocks on the gate, you can try something I’ve spent forty years overlooking:

Open it.

Essential Questions

  1. What parts of yourself are still waiting below the surface, hoping to be understood, before shared?

  2. How much of your identity was discovered through reflection? And how much through interaction?

item.title: Frequency and Repetition
item.description: On overthinking, invisible signals, and why repetition matters more than perfection.
item.dc:creator: Sean Forde
item.content:encoded:
I’ve been obsessed with “signals” lately. I feel like I’m looking at everything as if they’re signals.

I know, too much time in data . . .

It’s been helping me attend to things differently. Less fixed. Less finished. And lighter.

Specifically, it’s helping me rethink and follow interactions.

Normally, I’m so in my head about what to say or how to say it. Waste of time!

People communicate in signals. We are quite musical under the skin. And because of this, people respond first and foremost to the frequency and repetition of signals.

My Default Mode

I’m thinking all the time. I’m so in my head I have to actively summon myself to the surface when around others.

In a way, I’m over-inputting. There’s too many signals coming and I’m trying to understand them all.

Leaves me left pushing the wind bracing preparing how to enter the world.

Being in my head is a wonderful place. I love it there. I can think on my own terms. Sculpt it. Pressure test it. And send it out there, lovingly packaged, to someone.

That person hears it as a signal amongst a sea of signals, verbal and non. Even if they engage, it’ll likely be minimal in comparison to the thought and mental gymnastics I put it through.

You might wonder, why not just send smaller signals?

It’s an automatic thing. A fear that someone is going to take what I’ve done and misunderstand it or use it against me. There’s a fear that I’ll be judged now and forever by it. There’s a gravity to my default signals that needs to shift.

. . . frequency and repetition

The real wisdom in this is it doesn’t matter what the signal is like. If people are responding to the shape and intention of my signals, which have less to do with the content and more to do with me, I simply need to signal more.

And if all that’s required is more signals, not better ones, my default state is forced to reorient.

What’s Helping Me

I love guiding questions and affirmations. Here are the three I’ve been using recently:

  1. What’s the smallest visible signal you can send to someone?

  2. How can you keep up the momentum?

  3. If you know what you’re going to say, you’re ahead of the moment. Let your words surprise you.

In other words, it doesn’t matter if your signals are perfect or meaningful. Send em once and they’ll fade.

And truer still, a single signal rarely changes much on its own. Signals are not static. They need to be kept in motion if you want others to receive. And it all starts with

. . . frequency and repetition

Hey, even eye contact is a visible signal. It opens the channel.

Get seen, I’m telling myself. Get felt.

Essential Questions

  1. What are your signals mostly like when you are in a conversation? At work? With different friends and family members?

  2. Like I asked myself in the essay, “Why not just send smaller signals?”

item.title: Lessons Learned from Mario Ghosts
item.description: Some things only move when you stop watching.
item.dc:creator: Sean Forde
item.content:encoded:
You know the ghost in Mario games? You look and it disappears. Turn away and it chases you.

There’s wisdom in the way the two relate to one another.

Put simply, some things happen when we are attending. Other things happen when we are not. Attending could be as simple as paying attention, but it also includes actions with one’s eye on an outcome.

I’ve been attending too much.

Words, changes, tone, feelings. And in every shift, intentions are re-inferred.

And like in Mario, attending too closely or without breaking causes the momentum to evaporate. Like I’m not looking at reality anymore, but my perception of it, which exists only in transparent (projected) form.

I also used to think that if the ghost catches you, the ghost kills you. Really it just forces a choice (ok. maybe not for Mario, but for the human being playing the game). The choice is whether or not to replay the level.

But then, what’s the point of reaching the flag at the end? I would say it’s a marker showing you where you stand. In life, we place our own flags.

Right now I am learning to turn away from the ghost. Let it chase me.

item.title: Teaching Fish and Learning to Breathe
item.description: Learning to slow down, breathe deeper, and find direction without chasing goals. A reflection on curiosity, connection, visibility, and what it means to swim through change without losing yourself.
item.dc:creator: Sean Forde
item.content:encoded:
Curiosity,  connection,  and  visibility

   That’s  where  I’m   swimming   at    t h e s e     d a y s

So, a lot happened.

Ireland, two work trips, a new Salesforce working group, and my boss quitting. Basically, the universe’s way of saying, “you ain’t bored, right?”

Work has certainly got my head in a bit of a spin. With the ways my role is developing compounded by the change in management, it’s hard not to see the parallels. To see history repeating.

What’s radical to me, though, is more basic. I see it. This, alone, is also a sign I’m not in stress mode.

During this time, I have tried to frame all of these situations and experiences as opportunities. These trips were great opportunities to open up and connect with friends, family, and coworkers. And I’m trying to apply a different mindset to this Salesforce group. Something I can continue to grow into.

I have also been more intentional about reaching out to friends and I can feel a support system developing. About a month ago, I was feeling sad and I reached out by text to both a friend and my sister. It feels embarrassing to admit, but it’s just not something I do or have ever really done. Felt a bit like trespassing.

At first it was the, “No one wants to be bothered with my crap”.

Then, it became, “I want to be bothered with my crap. Aren’t I someone?”

Eventually, after sharing my feelings with others, it became, “Feels good to have someone to share crap with. Not just the sharing of my own, but the receiving of theirs too.” Then, naturally, I wonder if they feel the same way.

What Happened?

When I started medication for ADHD, everything slowed down. Considering the medication was a stimulant, this was very surprising to me. It’s like my body was previously speeding down some road while I was half-asleep steering just trying to avoid hitting things. Waking up alerted me to how fast I was going and the immediate effect was a downshifting in gears.

The next effect was a sharpness in moments. It’s like I was now in-sync with what was happening around me and could proceed with clarity. It was wild and still is. Driving at the same speed makes it easier to smile and connect with other drivers.

I’ve been diving into somatic and myofunctional therapy, along with the Alexander Technique. It’s a jumble that somehow works for me. After years of trying, I’ve finally retrained myself to breathe through my nose, and it’s changed everything. I’m sleeping better and moving through life at a slower, steadier pace.

What’s Fast Is Slow and What’s Slow Is Fast

I have long considered myself to be low-energy. I don’t say this as a judgment and my demeanor has typically been patient and even-tempered. Being this way has served me well.

As I develop more physical awareness, though, I find I can monitor my breathing better. With that comes an awareness of the tensions I carry all over my body: the postural impacts of a life of shrinking. Even accidents from long ago have left marks in the tensions my body carries and I’m finding myself finally able to release.

That’s the thing I’ve learned about stress mode. Your muscles tense and brace to keep you alive, which serves a purpose in the moment. But if the body remains in stress, the tensions stay put too. Eventually you find yourself held in the stone of your own armor.

As I practice my breathing and my stretching, I feel this steady release. It’s addicting. It’s got me stretching in meetings at work and everywhere I go. I’m sure I look like a weirdo but I’ve decided I don’t care. I’m on a mission to downshift as completely as I can. I’m done carrying the past.

The irony is this: As I release more and more tension, I’m gaining energy. It’s a strange notion, but one I’m trying to lean into. Essentially, I’m trying to relax into myself knowing the relaxation allows the me waiting underneath to emerge more fully.

Teaching a School of Fish

While I have lots to say about all of this, I’ve found myself coming back to nature and how things are held together. Maybe it was Ireland, I don’t know, but I keep coming back to fish in the ocean. Specifically, to a single metaphor.

That of a grown-up fish “teaching” a school of fish.

In this metaphor, one cannot imagine the fish teaching with a curriculum. Even if tied to essential skills and understandings, they presume things about the future. This is the hallmark of backward planning and it certainly has its place in strategic planning, but I’m finding myself drawn away from it. Towards something different.

In an ocean, I imagine fish are shown how to develop their own internal compass and scanning system. The compass points the direction and the scanning system is for awareness and action . . . and by extension interaction.

There’s no telling where in the ocean one might wind up a year from now and one’s needs and direction are inherently self-directed.

Do I Want Goals?

It also got me thinking about goals. What are a fish’s goals beyond survival?

Based on how fish behave in tanks, I imagine they enjoy comfortable or interesting environments and their nature to swim in groups suggests there’s some social awareness too.

Even though we are very different, I wonder if this metaphor has more in common with our world than we realize. To me, the world outside ourselves is a dynamic one and a fluid one. It is constantly changing to the point where one can never stay put.

If our focus shifts from goals and outcomes to the direction we embody, how should we understand the systems we live within?

As shared in earlier essays, I would argue that our society has encouraged compasses that point towards self-optimization and self-exploitation.

For myself, I am trying to reject this. I don’t want to say I’m rejecting goals altogether, but I am certainly prioritizing the present over the future. For myself, I have an emerging compass and I’m intentionally setting and reflecting upon it.

Curiosity, connection, and visibility. That’s where I’m swimming at these days.

These notions aren’t disconnected from the book idea. In fact, as I started writing it, I was overwhelmed with the many directions into which it was unfolding. The writing process is exciting and I don’t want to rush it. I would also like to take advantage of it as an opportunity to reflect on specific classes and moments from my career.

So what do I make of this publication? It’s called Resonance.

When I think about resonance, I think of frequency and space. Just as a singer’s vocal cavity amplifies loudness and richness, it only can happen when the two elements are present. All space with no frequency and you get unfulfilled potential; all frequency with no space and you get emotional energy trapped and unsettled.

I have things I want to say. I don’t know why I want to say them, but I need to get them out. For years, I’ve been singing these things to myself. Occasionally I share things online, but it’s often an album after years of work lumped into one or two posts.

Typically, I want my voice to sound good, for the recording to come out well, for the mix to be clear. I don’t think I’ve prioritized curiosity, connection, or visibility in a while. Looking back at it all, no longer in a state of stress, I’m seeing things more clearly.

I’m tired of feeling alone in the process.

I plan to take up space with my frequencies, starting with this publication. I don’t know what the next post will be. Maybe another reflection. Maybe a chapter from the book. Maybe just something creative like a song or a carving.

I’m letting go of goals. In this shifting world, I’d rather swim. Curiosity, connection, and visibility are my direction. And resonance, like this space, is the water itself: a place for me to surface. A reflection of who I am and what I care about.

  • What aspects of you present themselves more clearly when you are stressed?

  • What aspects of you present themselves more clearly when you are not stressed?

item.title: Becoming Visible: Writing Towards a Truer Self
item.description: A quiet view through a rain-speckled window. Nothing dramatic, just rooftops and trees blurred by water and light. A moment of stillness and presence, observing life without needing to control it.
item.dc:creator: Sean Forde
item.content:encoded:
So far, I’ve written about music, education, and what it means to feel seen while making space for others. Some of these are ideas I have thought a lot about during the past 20 years. Other ideas have come to me while I’m processing it all. At first I just wanted to tell my story. As my writing gains focus, though, I realize what’s happening. I didn’t plan for it to become a book. Not at first. But looking back on my first five posts, it feels to me like I am.

I came to Substack because I needed to do something. I was settling into a new career and finally had the space to reflect and really sit with what I had left. I’ve spent a lot of time caught in rumination, turning things over in my head, and never letting anyone in. I’ve spent even more time trying to stay in control of myself. Trying to be good. To do the right thing. For everybody else. But nowadays, I’m trying to act for myself and on my own accord. I’ve got to try on a different way of being me. My therapist would call this “taking action,” and this is me trying.

Putting Myself Out There

I’m not usually someone who easily lets others in. To see me, the real insecure and worried me. Recently, however, I’ve been trying. I’ve overcorrected at times, but I’m getting better and I’m committed to figuring it out. I’m often called calm, smart, helpful, kind. And I do believe I am those things. But some of it, if I’m honest, has calcified into performance. It insists upon itself, as Michelle would joke. It’s not that it’s fake. It’s just unembodied. Unchallenged. And ultimately unseen. I’ve lived inside this persona for so long it’s hard to know how to step outside of it.

It’s never been superficial or a lie. It was just borne out of fear and hiding. That’s the persona of someone who wants to remain invisible. To avoid being a burden. Who never asks for help and shrinks. Self-confidence has been a recent goal of mine, and it’s been hard. Harder than I thought it would be. I’ve hardened humility into something that hurts. And I’ve been rewarded for it, even admired at times. But as I zoom out on my life, I think it’s time I stop hiding behind these things. I don’t want to live like I’m just waiting around to die. And I don’t want to be so humble I disappear.

On that note, I also need connection. Visibility requires others. Deep down, I know that. I haven’t given myself many chances to explore what that could look like. And I haven’t given others that chance either. Maybe this post is one of them.

Learning to Stay Seen

What’s next? I want to keep going. I want to keep taking action. I want to finish this book, or whatever it’s becoming. I recently outlined what it might look like if it were fully fleshed out.

This is what I came up with:

Chapter 1: A Beginning: What I Left and Didn’t Leave Behind
Chapter 2: A New Commitment: Reclaiming Ourselves
Chapter 3: How Does Music Build Community
Chapter 4: Cultivating Presence: The Soil Between Us
Chapter 5: Curriculum Shaping: The Choice Between Conformity and Becoming
Chapter 6: Living the Curriculum: Designing Encounters
Chapter 7: Living the Curriculum: Relational Awareness
Chapter 8: Rethinking Assessment
Chapter 9: The Role of Teacher Imagination and Creativity
Chapter 10: The Death of the Teacher
Chapter 11: Living Beyond The Classroom (Recognizing Boundaries and Limitations)

I won’t pretend it’s perfect. All of it could change tomorrow. Maybe I’ll get writer’s block and this is all I got. Maybe I’ll forget and just move on to something else. I’m sharing all this because I’d like to live out in the open a bit more. At least for right now, this is where I am:

Wanting to live more fully, not muted or hedged with apologies, full of integrity, courage, and self-forgiveness. To do this, I know I need to loosen my grip on being “good,” “appropriate,” or “correct” and begin again, but now, with conviction.

Not because I know everything.

But because I’m here and I’m real.

Because that’s enough
