  • How have you changed by letting yourself be known?

  • What might it look like to live more fully? And who could you become if you did?

item.title: Curriculum Shaping: The Choice Between Conformity and Becoming
item.dc:creator: Sean Forde
item.content:encoded:
Curriculum is not neutral. It’s existential. It decides, in every objective, every standard, and every assessment, whether students will be reduced to outcomes or called to become subjects.

Most curricula are designed to control the paths of students. To deliver standards and to measure outcomes. A real curriculum, a human curriculum, must refuse this. It must leave spaces empty where the system demands they be filled, not to go without structure, but to reclaim it as something flexible and alive. Much of it comes down to awareness and priorities.

In every unit and lesson, the real question is not “What will students learn?” The real question is: Who will they become?

Flashback:

Second year of teaching. A November afternoon in the computer lab. It’s my lunch period, but I’m not eating. Instead, I’m hunched over a keyboard, retyping a curriculum to appease my administrators. Around me, students loiter. A few are genuinely curious, but most are just avoiding their work. One leans over and asks, “Hey Mr. Forde. What are you writing?”

I don’t remember what I told them, but I do remember the feeling. Pinned. Like the walls of the school were closing in.

A week earlier, I had been observed by one of my assistant principal and her feedback was blunt: not rigorous enough. The students were focused on singing and instruments, which didn’t align with her expectations. She told me, proudly, that she was tone-deaf, and that not everyone "gets" music. I think she was trying to curtail my idealism. “And anyway”, she added, “everyone needs Social Studies for the state test”.

Couldn’t I connect my lessons to the Erie Canal or The Star-Spangled Banner? Couldn’t I model my reflection questions after those found on state tests. I tried to push back, gentle and polite. I said I believed every child could learn to sing and create. But it didn’t matter. I was there to produce outcomes. Outcomes that she considered more legitimate.

Sitting in that computer lab, surrounded by my students, the very ones I was being asked to betray, I rewrote my curriculum. Not because I believed in it or because it would serve them. But because the school demanded it. And I compromised. All the while secretly proceeding as I was.

I’ve known many teachers who live this double life: the official curriculum for the observers, the real curriculum for the students. But this double curriculum is not a clever workaround. It’s a wound. Every day teachers are asked to undo themselves little by little, in the name of “rigor” and “accountability.”

This is the reality of modern teaching: to avoid being excessed, hassled, or bullied, we violate the very purpose that brought us here. And we call it "rigor." We call it "standards." We call it "best practice."

What it really is . . . is surrender.

The Lie of Preparedness

I entered teaching with a degree and a handful of college-drafted lessons. Once in a school, though, a colder reality set in. No instruments. No whiteboard. Not even doors that lock. Just me, an auditorium full of children, and the requirement that I succeed . . . or else be held responsible for limiting the opportunities that those children deserved.

In many ways, I was never set up for success. Most teachers aren’t.

But the truth is, I was set up to fail long before that first day. First, in the very institutions that are supposed to prepare us. Teacher preparation programs spend months on theory and methods, but avoid curriculum design. There’s a fear that if teachers learn to write curricula, they will be less responsive and more likely to run on autopilot. What they fail to see is that without this preparation, teachers are not free to thrive; they are left unequipped.

And schools are no better at this. They demand curriculum. They demand artifacts. They demand coverage. But they provide no time to plan it and no support to sustain it. You are told to align to standards, to differentiate instruction, and to prove results, but no one shows you how to actually build the thing that holds it all together. It’s assumed it will simply come with experience. But why are we leaving this all to hope? Can’t we dive into the messiness without prescription?

The result is predictable. Teachers are left to scavenge for ideas on their own time. And when the curriculum fails or when the students struggle, the teacher alone is blamed. This is not freedom or accountability. This is abandonment masquerading as autonomy.

Those first lessons carried me through September, but by mid-October, I was empty. I had no ideas and no margin for error. So I did what teachers are expected to do. I improvised. I tried out songs from old books. I tried out songs the kids shared with me. I copied activities from websites and collected anything that looked like it might fill time. I built a patchwork syllabus out of desperation and thin air. Spoiler alert: it didn’t work.

The students were not progressing, the classes felt unmanageable, and my plans turned out to be hollow. When I looked around for help, I found nothing real or useful. Online “curricula” offered wonderfully worded objectives and neat timelines, but they too were written for students who didn’t exist. They assumed too much. They assumed cultural capital. They assumed a past my students didn’t have.

By June, I had scrapped two failed curricula and assembled a third. This one was more clearly connected to state standards and New York City’s Blueprint for the Arts. Not because it served my students, but because it would satisfy my administrators.

It was a stronger document, but it wasn’t a curriculum. It was a performance. I was translating the living work of music educators into the dead language of outcomes. Unsettled by this, I spent the next five years in a different kind of desperation. I wanted something real and I wanted something useful.

I bought used books with the little money I had. I studied Kodály’s sequences. I explored Orff’s creative play. I combed through Feierabend’s musical fluency and Gordon’s theories of audiation. I pulled ideas from Little Kids Rock, Carnegie Hall, McGraw-Hill, and Silver Burdett.

I was never offered a curriculum. Instead, I was left to invent one, to stitch it together out of fragments. Not because anyone asked me to, but because getting through the school year demanded it.

What I didn’t see then, and what is painfully clear now, is that the act of shaping a curriculum was changing me. Every map I created, every plan I reworked, was a wager. A wager on what kind of teacher I could be. And a wager on what kind of human beings my students might become.

Curriculum was not just logistics. It was imagination. It was structured resistance.

A human curriculum, even one trying to foment resistance, still needs structure. So do teachers and students. They each need their own rituals, their own landmarks in time, otherwise, the year is long and can break a person. The key is to use structure to your advantage, not as confinement, but as scaffolding. Students need challenges and they need routines. And everyone needs clear pathways to deepen their craft as well as their humanity. The real task is to create a structure that bends toward becoming.

Having shared some of these frustrations with other music teachers, it has become apparent that my story is not unique. In the arts, and especially in underfunded schools, teachers are regularly abandoned. They are left to construct futures from nothing and then blamed when those futures don’t fit the system. The same flawed system that was never built to value creativity, difference, or humanity in the first place.

This is why arts teachers guard their curricula with such ferocity. It’s not a binder or a set of lesson plans. It’s a lifeline. It’s a collection of hard-won survival strategies. An accumulated memory of every risk.

If you are fortunate, if you are stubborn enough, a curriculum can become something else. It can become rebellion and it can also become freedom.

Each summer, while others assumed I was resting, I sat alone with the exhaustion of the year, reflected and read. I reread Gordon’s Learning Sequences. I revisited Freire’s Pedagogy of the Oppressed. I returned to Dewey’s Experience and Education, Palmer’s The Courage to Teach, and Lyotard’s The Postmodern Condition. For me, these weren’t academic exercises. They were rituals.

No one assigned them. No one asked and no one noticed. But I knew, subconsciously, that if I didn’t reclaim my purpose, the system would erase it before the first bell rang in September. Curriculum writing was not just summer work. It was preservation. It was the only way I knew to keep from being hollowed out.

Curriculum, at its best, is not about delivering content. It’s about helping students, through your subject area, to fully realize their selfhood.

Gert Biesta indicts the entire enterprise of modern schooling, framing it around two primary purposes: qualification and socialization. Schools teach students the skills they need to be useful, and the norms they must follow to fit in. These are necessary, perhaps, but they are not sufficient.

Beyond these is a third educational purpose: subjectification. It’s a slower and more unpredictable process where a human being becomes a subject. Not an object of someone else's design and not a product shaped to meet demands. But a person who can stand in the world with freedom and responsibility. Someone who understands what the world is calling them to be and who can choose whether or not, as well as how, to answer it. Subjectification cannot be commanded. It cannot be scheduled. It can only be invited.

Real curriculum, then, cannot be an assembly line. It’s not what we plan for students to become, but the possibility that they will become someone we can’t yet imagine. Curriculum, in this light, is never a guarantee. It’s a risk we take on their behalf.

And on ours.

Following the Students

At the end of my first year, I made the most dangerous decision a teacher can make. I asked my elementary students what they thought of my class and my teaching. What did they like? What did they hate? What mattered?

They didn’t give me data. They gave me moments. They shared memories. They taught me what no curriculum guide ever could: that the work is not to cover content. The work is to help them uncover themselves.

Curriculum, it was clear, cannot be fully mapped. Not even if I had written it for the needs of my students. It must be an opening. It must leave margins blank and moments unfinished. It must refuse the bureaucratic fantasy of “bell-to-bell instruction”.

In my first years, I was filling time. I packed my lessons with activities I thought the students would love, believing that if I could just control every minute, the students would have no choice but to learn and to love music. But beneath the control was fear. Fear that if I left anything unprepared, I would lose them. Fear that chaos would take the class.

By my fifth year, the binders were still there on the shelf, but I stopped looking at them. They were relics of a teaching ideology I no longer believed. Each group of students took what I did in different directions. What remained was not a system, but a practice of inviting, listening, and responding.

Nel Noddings understood this. Education, she wrote, is not a transaction. It is not the delivery of content or the achievement of standards. It is a relationship. It’s a dangerous and necessary relationship between two beings, each vulnerable, each incomplete.

Care, for Noddings, is not kindness. It is attention. The kind of attention that does not measure or predict, and doesn’t even prepare a reply. The kind of attention that risks being changed by what it witnesses. To plan with care is not to prepare for efficiency, but for encounters.

In making space, a real curriculum cannot be designed primarily to produce achievement. It must be designed to allow teachers and students to meet and to matter.

Learning begins there. In that meeting. Or it doesn’t begin at all.

Time and Tension: Curriculum as Compass, Not a Clock

It’s easy to blame standards alone for the failures of modern schooling. But the problem isn’t having standards. It’s how we have allowed them to multiply, escalate, and harden to address “under-performing” systems.

It’s interesting how people justify raising standards in schools. We say it’s to compete with other nations. We say we want students to learn what we were taught as if that was inherently better. And we often fail to notice dominant narratives baked into these expectations. Assuming the best intentions, standards can certainly offer a floor, a shared language, or a starting point. But floors are not horizons. And education cannot be reduced to a race toward checkpoints.

Most curriculum today is built backwards intentionally. It begins with standards and ends with outcomes. Everything is packaged into timelines that assume learning can be scheduled. This is the delivery system Noddings and Biesta warned against.

Curriculum, if we take it seriously, exists in contradictory spaces. Every moment of teaching demands an impossible choice: structure or freedom, guidance or trust, plan or presence. And decisions like this, which would be difficult with a single student, must be scaled to address the needs of 30 students or more at a time. Pretending this isn’t impossible, or that a perfect balance can be struck if only the teacher were “effective” enough, is a lie we tell ourselves to align with the system.

A curriculum can’t just be a map with time stamped outcomes. It must be a compass, chunked across time, and with potential ideas. A compass doesn’t dictate a path. It orients you. It tells you where you are facing and reminds you of direction, even when the terrain shifts. And in education, the terrain is always shifting. A compass also doesn’t deliver anything. It reminds you which way is north so you can choose for yourself your next steps.

But even this critique, even this refusal of tidy sequenced maps, is not enough.

Byung-Chul Han reminds us that modern schooling is not just a machine of conformity. The achievement society, he claims, no longer demands obedience. It demands self-exploitation. We no longer need to be watched because we watch ourselves. Students too. They don’t simply conform for us, they perform for us too. They package themselves for grades, tests, auditions, and applications. They optimize their time, their talents, and even their identities for visibility and success. And if they don’t, we take the stage.

This, let’s be clear, is an even deeper betrayal. Backward-mapped curricula, built to meet standards, don’t have to be the problem, but when their outcomes and rubrics are framed too heavily around rigor, performance, or student independence, they are complicit. They are instruments of an achievement driven society. They turn students into projects and learning into labor. Am I good enough, thinks the student? Am I good enough, thinks the teacher? As students stare down behavior charts and teachers perform for observation rubrics, what sort of presence do we really expect to form around such relationships?

Success now is not just submission. It’s burnout dressed up as diligence. Compliance becomes self-sufficiency and we tell ourselves it’s freedom.

Han, like Noddings, calls us back to something more radical: attention. Not an efficient attention like spot checking. Not productive attention like running records either. But uncomfortable attention to the other refusing to define or categorize.

Curriculum, if it is to matter, must offer opportunities for achievement while refusing the machinery of achievement society. It must reject the fantasy of optimization.

The Myth of Student-Led = Chaos

There is a popular myth about student-led learning. That it means letting students do whatever they want. That it leads to anarchy. That structure collapses and that learning anything “boring” or necessary disappears. This is a lie.

True student-led learning is not absence of instruction. Teachers set the initial conditions, offer the first songs, guide the discussions, and adjust the sails. They don’t relinquish responsibility. They share it.

Real student-led learning is not a collapse of structure. It’s just a different structure. One built on trust, dialogue, and mutual attention. In my own classroom, I found the most powerful structures were not plans or policies, but questions. I posted them on the walls. I wove them into google slides and word docs. I planned them into every lesson. Essential Questions were not decorations. They were my invitations. They were real questions to spark my student’s thinking and provoke attention.

Questions are not just a technique. They are an ethical stance. They resist the urgency to direct, to finish, or to assess. They leave space for something unplanned to emerge.

Lucy Green’s work on informal music learning reminds us that the most powerful learning often looks, to an outsider, like failure. It’s messy, unsupervised, and aimless, but beneath that mess is agency. Students learn best, not when they are controlled, but when they are trusted to embrace themselves. They learn not just skills, but how to decide which skills matter.

Informal learning is more humane. It’s more real. And it can be more transformative.

Randall Allsup goes further. He reminds us that true teaching must unsettle authority itself. This isn’t to eliminate the teacher’s role, but to dismantle the delivery system and replace it with a shared, emergent journey. Curriculum, in this view, is never a finished product. It is an invitation to walk together, without knowing exactly where the path will lead.

Informal learning, real dialogue, and shared inquiry. These are the hallmarks of what I found worked. Really worked. These are not techniques for better management. They are conditions for something much harder . . . embracing education as a lived experience.

The Planning Paradox - Navigating Tensions

Where does this leave us? With some difficult and necessary truths.

Teachers must prepare. Deeply. Carefully. Rigorously. And they must also be ready to leave that preparation behind the moment the classroom demands it. But preparation and presence are not opposites to be balanced. They can be complementary and they can be contradictory. Either way, there is a tension at play. And wherever there is tension, we are called to respond with conviction. Teaching is full of tension.

These tensions aren’t mistakes to fix or gaps to fill. They are core to the work itself and they must be navigated:

  • Structure and Freedom: The tension between providing dependable guidance and honoring student agency.

  • Planning and Presence: The tension between thoughtful preparation and staying open to what emerges in the moment.

  • Standards and Emergence: The tension between shared expectations and allowing space for unexpected insights.

  • Accountability and Authenticity: The tension between meeting collective goals and expressing genuine individuality.

  • Activity and Integration: The tension between diving into action, movement or creation, and providing space to absorb and make meaning.

None of these are battles to be won. None of them have a correct side. Each tension holds a truth. Each side serves a purpose. And it is the willingness to live inside these tensions without rushing to resolve them that defines real teaching.

Schools, for their part, prefer order. They prefer compliance, visible routines, and proof that learning is happening. It is the role of the teacher to bring the class back into these tensions. To recognize that these tensions are not flaws. That they are the medium through which learning becomes possible.

And under all of these tensions lies a deeper, unavoidable truth.

In every plan there is the risk that no one will learn.
In every risk there is the possibility that someone will become.

As mentioned earlier, teaching is a wager. Even the best plans can leave students unmoved. And even the clumsiest moments can ignite something that lasts a lifetime. This is not an argument against preparation, but again for conviction. For humility. For courage. And for remembering that teaching and learning are not the same thing. This is not a cause and effect process that can be measured no matter how hard our society tries.

Curriculum is not certainty. It never has been. It’s important to remember that when you read other people’s curricula. It is always relational risk. It’s an art of setting things in motion and being willing to follow the living energy of the classroom.

With this in mind, I’ll present an idea for a curriculum, not as some model others should follow, but to share a different way of thinking. Here is a glimpse of a unit for classes that had music once every week.

The Heavier Weight of Freedom

There’s a price to this kind of teaching. It’s much harder than control. It’s messier, and lonelier too. And usually, it’s less celebrated. No one will hand you a gold star for resisting the status quo and no one will congratulate you for refusing to perform.

But here’s where I see opportunity. Universities will not hand you the tools and schools will not give you the time. Curriculum work is largely invisible and impossible to measure. And when you struggle, because you will, you will not be rescued. You will be blamed.

And worse, you won’t always know if you’re succeeding. You won’t always be able to point to evidence. You will labor in a space where success can’t always be seen or scaled.

But what you create, in its place, will be real. It will be human. And if you are lucky, and can bear this weight, it will be enough.

Closing: Sisyphus in the Classroom

Camus reminds us: One must imagine Sisyphus happy.

I think of that often. Those afternoons in the computer lab, piecing together plans that would inevitably unravel. Plans to accommodate the absurdity of my situation.

Why did I stay, you may wonder? I’ve asked myself that many times. Early on, I reached out to coworkers for help. They were kind, but they had their own burdens, and when it came to the arts, they weren’t enough. I reached out to one of my favorite professors. Her advice was to find another school.

It was good advice, but it was 2008 and jobs were scarce. Maybe that’s an excuse. I don’t know, but I stayed. Not because the work would save me. It was never meant to. I stayed because the trying mattered.

I was never going to master it or finish it. But meeting it fully. Again and again. And with care. It mattered to me.

That is what curriculum, at its best, can be:

A preparation not for conformity or answers, but for becoming.

  • In your life or work, what structures support your becoming rather than limit it?

item.title: Cultivating Presence: The Soil Between Us
item.description: What if presence isn’t just a nice idea, but the ground we grow from?This essay explores imposter syndrome, education, and the radical act of showing up as you are.
item.dc:creator: Sean Forde
item.content:encoded:
“The most precious gift we can offer anyone is our attention. When mindfulness embraces those we love, they will bloom like flowers.”

― Thich Nhat Hanh

I still remember that afternoon. Driving in the rain from school, changing into my suit in the car, and running inside to an interview at a mortgage company. Pulse quickening as I entered the lobby, seeing I was about 10 minutes late. I had called en route, but here I was in front of the receptionist, still apologizing, eager yet uncertain. Moments later, I was told the position I was interviewing for was no longer available. Just as my stomach dropped, a man named Tom stepped forward, curious about my background in technology and my interest in instructional design. He asked me to step into a nearby office and we began discussing my resume. The conversation shifted, and by the time I left, I had the job with Tom as my manager. A roller coaster day that ended in elation.

Initially, my time at the organization felt strange. I wasn’t just a fish out of water, I was a fish learning to walk. I had to master an industry I knew next to nothing about, starting with their self-directed online program, Xinnix. It was painfully dry and went on forever. Dense slides of regulations, exhausting financial jargon, and few meaningful hands-on activities. Imagine a set of e-learning compliance modules that went on for over two weeks. Yet, I pressed on, held together by hope, and a need to prove myself.

A few weeks in, there came two unexpected conversations. First, Tom informed me he was leaving. It was the result of a disagreement with the CEO. "I’m not coming back," he said angrily, completely shaking my sense of security. Shortly after, still a bit paralyzed, the CEO asked me into his office and offered me surprising freedom: "Forget that guy! The office is yours. Learn every role: price loans, process loans, close loans. Try it all." What else would I say? Of course I said sure. I suppose this fish now had to learn to fly.

Panic surged. Here I stood, an outsider expected to teach others a job I barely grasped myself. And before I could do that, I would have to cold call potential borrowers, assess their income stability, and clear underwriting conditions. My imposter syndrome had never felt more intense. But rather than freeze, I chose to show up authentically. I sat with a number of employees, documenting their processes, asking genuine questions, and getting to know them along with their roles. I didn’t seek to impress, but was honest about what I didn’t know, and remained curious. After a few months of this, I designed experience-based, scenario-driven training sessions, stepping alongside my coworkers into unfamiliar terrain. I found some solace and inspiration in Jacques Rancière’s The Ignorant Schoolmaster. It helped me embrace the vulnerability of learning openly alongside my peers.

In this messy, relational approach, I stumbled onto a profound realization: true learning doesn’t hinge on expertise. Really, it thrives in spaces of mutual presence, co-exploration, and shared emergence.

Presence in Unfamiliar Terrain

At this organization, my lack of expertise wasn’t a deficit. It was an invitation. Rather than pretend to be some sort of authority, I modeled authenticity and curiosity. By openly learning alongside others, I set a few precedents:

  1. It’s ok to admit what we don’t know

  2. We all have inherent value and have the ability to realize the best in ourselves

In short, I tried to remain present. By presence, I don’t just mean physically being there or paying attention. I mean a full embodied engagement with myself, others, and the moment. A kind of openness that invites growth, not performance.

Traditional education often centers on developing skills and passing content on to the learner. When teaching elementary music, I knew I had to be more active and experiential in making this happen. It would have been too rigid otherwise as the kids were fidgety and wanted to move. I assumed adults were different, and of course they are, but a more relational approach, the only approach I knew, seemed to transcend age.

It was easy to see how the deepest learning would never come from those boring e-learning modules. What was needed was something relaxed in pressure but firm in honest curiosity. In dialogue, and a mutual form of witnessing, we generated insights collectively. Something no slide deck could capture. I remember when the quieter loan officers began asking me questions they were too afraid to ask more senior members of the team. The organization’s culture was heavy on execution, but that left little space to try, fail, and try again a little differently. Relational learning is more immediate, contextualized, and fundamentally human driven.

Imposter Syndrome as Catalyst

I’m sure I had a calm exterior as I typically do, but believe me when I say I was freaking out on the inside. I felt so inadequate, but my anxiety actually became a powerful motivator. It kept me humble, engaged, and extremely present (hyper-alert perhaps). The anxiety I felt teaching at an elementary school was more systemic and could be debated, at least intellectually, with my aforementioned “expertise”. If the expectations were creating problems, I could assert myself more confidently because in music, I felt that I knew best. And at my school, I did.

Feeling unqualified, however, pushed me to seek connection rather than control. I don't think anxiety is a necessity. In fact, it can do way more harm than good. But in this particular case, I think it amplified a need to connect in a way I hadn’t felt before.

Witnessing as Emergence

Tom’s abrupt departure was more than a turning point. It felt almost mythic, as if the ground beneath me shifted. His leaving forced a choice I couldn’t put off. At the time, I would have much preferred he stayed; that he could have guided me in a structured manner. There’s comfort in structure. That’s what I always wanted to provide my students. But that’s not how it played out. I was new to a job and had to figure it out on my own. In a bizarre way, it felt similar to how I had to figure everything out at my school. Here, though, I came with even less preparation, or so I thought.

Bottom line, I could shrink back into my fears or step forward, visible and vulnerable. Choosing to step forward, I became visible not only to others but also to myself. And as I witnessed my own growth, I saw how deeply interconnected presence and courage really are.

Tending the Soil

In my post, "A New Commitment: Reclaiming Ourselves," I explored what I called the "negative space between us". These were the assumptions, expectations, and power dynamics in our interactions. This negative space isn't merely an encroaching emptiness or something against which to fight back; it’s a fertile ground where systems, culture, and internal narratives can grow. Presence, then, is about consciously and actively cultivating this negative space, making it visible and intentional. It’s soil that we tend. And it’s where genuine connection, belonging, and individual emergence can occur.

Presence, when seen as a form of tending to this space, helps us to be more responsive. It does seem to fly in the face of preparedness, but it doesn’t have to. I believe it’s possible, and ideal, to be both prepared and present, but being present may sometimes ask us to throw away our plans . . . with intention. When we don’t, or are unwilling to do so, our plans become their own micromanagers. The consequence, in my experience, is a shrinking of the individual and a diminished sense of self-worth.

A Worth Beyond Achievement

Let’s be really clear. Our worth is inherent. Even at our absolute worst moments, we are enough and we are all deserving of that reminder. Whether it’s our strengths or capabilities, or simply our humanness with all its varied beauty and potential, our worth remains. When self-worth isn’t named or acknowledged as inherent, our systems imply a narrative that it is conditional. Byung Chul-Han points out that in today’s society, our focus on achievement, positivity, and even self-improvement fosters this conditional thinking. Even worse than in previous times, however, the blame has shifted from systemic blame to self-blame. Perhaps that’s a consequence of growing individualism. To cultivate what is needed for emergence, we need to acknowledge our full selves. Just as mindfulness can help us to stay aware and regulated, presence provides a place from which we can act as our fullest self. And the real kicker is in the way it allows others to be their full selves too.

I am speaking mostly as an educator or a person who leads, but really, this is just as crucial for our students. We all exist in the same classroom space. Don’t we? And like Rancière explains in The Ignorant Schoolmaster, there’s an equality of intelligences if we are brave enough to recognize it.

How I’ve Tried to Cultivate Presence

This isn’t a perfect system and I still have a lot to learn. It’s just a few things I return to when I need to ground myself, reconnect, or just slow down. Each one helps me stay more in the moment, more open, and more connected to myself and others.

Physiological
Feeling safe and settled in the body.
When I’m anxious, I start by noticing my breath, and take long exhales. Sometimes stretching helps too. I especially love breathwork and taking quiet walks to clear some of the static. The goal isn’t just calm, it’s awareness.

Perceptual
Paying attention to what’s happening through the senses.
I try to notice without naming. The light on the wall. The noise of the cars outside. As a songwriter, I’ve used Pat Pattison’s object writing exercises to lean into this. When I’m really present, I feel more alive to what’s around me and less trapped in my analysis or reaction.

Philosophical
Letting things be unfinished or unresolved.
This one's the hardest for me. I’m a pathological perfectionist and I want things to make sense, to feel clear. But presence here means not rushing to fix. It means letting things be messy. It means allowing space (for the moment, the feeling, the person) to exist without judgment or explanation.

Relational
Being with others in a real, unguarded way.
This shows up when I listen without preparing my response. When I pause instead of filling silence. When I let people ask me things I don’t have polished answers for. It also means letting others see me, even if I’m not sure how I’ll come across. Letting myself be seen is also a major challenge of mine.

Integrity
Showing up as myself. Not the role, not the mask.
This is more of a periodic check-in: Am I being honest right now? Am I doing something because it feels like I “should”? Who am I really?

These layers aren’t steps. They intertwine and they nurture my self-worth and depth in relationships. They don’t make me “better,” but they do make me more here and now.

None of this, I should point out, is new. Lots of this stuff is common knowledge in other mindfulness practices or therapeutic environments. In terms of education, however, I don’t think we’ve fully embraced these ideas and how they may be embodied by educators and students. And as for pedagogical philosophy, I don’t think we’ve followed these ideas through to their full implications. Gert Biesta, I find, has come closer than most.

Presence, Education, and Subjectification

Gert Biesta has greatly shaped my views on education. I came to his work late in my career, but found his ideas absolutely profound and reconciling of many progressive threads I had previously tried to enact. He emphasizes subjectification, or the process through which individuals emerge as autonomous, thinking beings, not merely products of societal expectations. True educational spaces invite students to become subjects, not objects of the learning process. Presence, then, isn’t just an educational tool; it’s the medium where subjectification can unfold authentically.

The reason this matters so much to me is because presence feels actively hindered by the systems in which teachers teach. Having worked now outside the school system, I see this is far bigger than just what goes on in schools. Bureaucratic systems may feel it differently, in a more cold and draconian manner, but the pressures exist in many systems. I suppose in a sick way, our focus on career readiness is working. It just never asked if these careers came with lives worth living.

Music, or the performing arts more broadly, offer a way out! Rather than mimicking broader compliance systems, true musical communities embrace shared creation, improvisation, and mutual witnessing. These environments, inherently messy and relational, nurture genuine subjectification and human connection.

I won’t pretend to be neutral. I am absolutely biased. What follows are convictions shaped by experience, not just opinion:

  • I believe that all school subjects offer opportunities to develop necessary life skills and understandings as well as ways to understand each other, ourselves, and the world around us.

  • I also believe that all school subjects are deserving of support and should be supported if we are to educate “the whole child”. For this to happen, I believe we should soften our approach to assessing STEM and ELA classes and start paying more attention to other subject areas like music, art, gym, etc. This belief isn’t just to be nice and care about every subject. I saw teachers regularly hitting diminishing marginal returns every time we added more math, science, tech, and literacy class periods and interventions to the school day. Ex: Kids who struggle in math typically get . . . more math. Wouldn’t it be a better use of the students time to find success in another subject area as opposed to doubling down on what are perceived as weaknesses?

  • I also believe that the performing arts stand out among disciplines. While all subject areas are essential in different ways, the arts offer the most potential for experiences that are engaging, challenging, creative, pluralist, responsive, and affective. The performing arts are unique in their temporal, experiential nature as well as in their power to build community. After all, you rarely hear of a painting ensemble. These qualities make it uniquely equipped, in my opinion, to develop caring, expressive people who are prepared for life. It can lead to lots of opportunities for joy or success and that too is no small thing.

Shifting the Measures

Ultimately, presence isn’t a goal. It’s the medium in which genuine learning, artistry, and belonging flourish. As educators and humans, our task isn't to impose growth, or set learning objectives, but to cultivate environments where presence emerges naturally, enriching each individual and the collective whole.

Our lives unfold in moments, not timelines. Let us all put down our measuring sticks, opening to our inner worlds and then extending that openness to each other. This is how we can create living webs of presence in all our relationships.

Join the conversation

If you’ve read this far, I’d love to hear from you.
